title: Day 4 — Supervised Learning.Logistic Regression
text:
Day 4 — Supervised Learning.Logistic Regression
These are the exercises for one teaching day of Module 3 of the Health Data Science MSc. Each chapter is one exercise you can finish in a single sitting, with an R path and a Python path doing the same work. Pick one; in class we go through R most of the time.
Some tasks appear as code containing ______ for you to fill in. They are shown but not run, which is why no output appears beneath them. The worked answers are published after the session.

title: Exercise 4.1 — One workflow, two classifiers
text:
In Exercise 3.1 you predicted a number, blood glucose. Now the outcome is a class: does this person have diabetes, pos or neg? The steps are exactly the same: specify a model, fit it on the training patients, and predict for new ones. Two things are new:

the specification says the model is for classification;
the prediction can be a probability for each class, as well as the class itself.










Exercise 3.1: glucose, a number
Exercise 4.1: diabetes, a class




specify (R)
linear_reg(), decision_tree() with set_mode("regression")
logistic_reg(), decision_tree() with set_mode("classification")


specify (Python)
LinearRegression(), DecisionTreeRegressor()
LogisticRegression(), DecisionTreeClassifier()


fit
fit() / .fit()
the same


predict
a number
a class, or a probability for each class




Part 1. Predict diabetes from glucose with a logistic regression. Get the probability and the class for one patient, see the patient on the fitted curve, and compare the predictions with what was measured in the test patients.
Part 2. Add BMI and predict for the same patient again. See the probability as a map over glucose and BMI.
Part 3. Keep the same steps, training patients and predictors, and fit a decision tree instead. Follow the patient to a leaf, read the probability and the class there, and compare the tree’s map with the logistic regression’s.







NoteThe plots are for looking at



The code for the plots is folded away under Code for this plot (optional). You do not need to write it, but it is in the download if you want it.



RPython


Download this exercise as an R Markdown notebook (.Rmd): the text and every code cell of the R version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "rpart.plot"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart.plot)

theme_set(theme_bw())

data/diabetes_clean.csv holds 750 adults screened for type 2 diabetes: eight measurements from a single visit, and diabetes, which is pos or neg. It is ready to use. We keep glucose, BMI (the column mass) and the outcome. If you do not have it yet, download diabetes_clean.csv into your data folder.

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(glucose, mass, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

summary(diabetes)

#>     glucose           mass       diabetes 
#>  Min.   : 57.0   Min.   :18.20   neg:477  
#>  1st Qu.:101.0   1st Qu.:27.80   pos:273  
#>  Median :119.0   Median :32.80            
#>  Mean   :125.5   Mean   :32.89            
#>  3rd Qu.:145.0   3rd Qu.:37.00            
#>  Max.   :196.0   Max.   :59.40


The outcome is a factor with two levels, neg then pos. The probabilities are then about pos: having diabetes.
We hold back every fifth person as the test set: 600 training patients and 150 test patients. Splitting by a fixed rule rather than at random gives both languages the same 150 people. Every Day 4 exercise uses this split.

test_rows <- seq(1, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)     # every fifth person is held back
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[test_rows, ]

count(train, diabetes)

#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   diabetes     n
#>   <fct>    <int>
#> 1 neg        380
#> 2 pos        220




Part 1 — Predict diabetes from glucose
The same three steps as in Exercise 3.1. The only change in the specification is the mode: classification instead of regression.

# 1. Specify: logistic regression, computed by glm(), for classification
log_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# 2. Fit on the training patients
log_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = train)

# the learned parameters: intercept first, then the weight for glucose
log_fit$fit$coefficients

#> (Intercept)     glucose 
#> -5.06398801  0.03502657


The two parameters are not on the glucose scale but on the log-odds scale. Exercise 4.2 shows how they turn into a probability. Here we let predict() do it.

Task 1a — A patient with a glucose of 150
predict() gives the class by default. With type = "prob" it gives a probability for each class instead.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
patient <- data.frame(glucose = 150)

predict(log_fit, new_data = patient, type = "______")   # a probability for each class
predict(log_fit, new_data = patient)                     # the class







TipStuck?





The word in quotes is short for probability.



The class is the probability cut at 0.5: pos if \(\hat{P}(\text{pos}) > 0.5\), neg otherwise. The red point is the patient, on the fitted curve:


Code for this plot (optional)
curve <- data.frame(glucose = seq(40, 200, by = 1))
curve$prob <- predict(log_fit, new_data = curve, type = "prob")$.pred_pos

ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = train, aes(x = glucose, y = as.numeric(diabetes == "pos")),
              width = 0, height = 0.03, alpha = 0.3, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(data = curve, aes(x = glucose, y = prob), colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("point", x = 150,
           y = predict(log_fit, new_data = patient, type = "prob")$.pred_pos,
           colour = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Probability of diabetes",
       title = "Training patients (0 = neg, 1 = pos), the fitted curve, and the patient")















ImportantThink about it




The model says pos for this patient. How sure is it?
At about what glucose does the predicted class change from neg to pos?





Task 1b — Predictions against what was measured
The test patients were not used to fit the model. Predict both the probability and the class for each of them, and put them next to what was measured.

test_results <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(log_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(log_fit, new_data = test))

head(test_results, 10)

#> # A tibble: 10 × 6
#>    glucose  mass diabetes .pred_neg .pred_pos .pred_class
#>      <dbl> <dbl> <fct>        <dbl>     <dbl> <fct>      
#>  1     194  28.5 neg          0.150     0.850 pos        
#>  2     117  30.1 pos          0.724     0.276 neg        
#>  3     122  57.3 neg          0.688     0.312 neg        
#>  4     111  26.8 neg          0.764     0.236 neg        
#>  5     142  39.5 pos          0.523     0.477 neg        
#>  6     102  28.9 neg          0.816     0.184 neg        
#>  7     111  37.7 neg          0.764     0.236 neg        
#>  8     101  35.4 neg          0.821     0.179 neg        
#>  9     112  36.6 neg          0.758     0.242 neg        
#> 10     142  37.4 neg          0.523     0.477 neg


How often is the predicted class right? Compare it with a “model” that always says neg, the most common class.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
mean(test_results$.pred_class == test_results$______)   # accuracy of the model
mean(test_results$diabetes == "neg")                    # always saying neg







TipStuck?





Compare the predicted class with the column that holds what was measured.





Code for this plot (optional)
ggplot(test_results, aes(x = glucose, y = .pred_pos, colour = diabetes)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(neg = "steelblue", pos = "darkorange")) +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Predicted probability of diabetes",
       colour = "Measured",
       title = "Test patients: predicted probability, coloured by what was measured")















ImportantThink about it




Every point lies on the same curve. What has the model got wrong for the orange points below the dashed line, and for the blue points above it?
Which is more useful to a clinician: the class, or the probability?






Part 2 — Add BMI
The same specification, log_model, with a second predictor:

log_fit_2 <- log_model |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass, data = train)

log_fit_2$fit$coefficients

#> (Intercept)     glucose        mass 
#> -7.00363758  0.03355403  0.06437328



Task 2a — The same patient, now with a BMI of 30

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
patient <- data.frame(glucose = 150, mass = ______)

predict(log_fit_2, new_data = patient, type = "______")
predict(log_fit_2, new_data = patient)







TipStuck?





The patient now needs a value for both predictors. Ask for the probabilities exactly as in Task 1a.



With two predictors, the probability is a map over glucose and BMI. The black line is where the probability is exactly 0.5: to its right the class is pos, to its left neg. Circles are test patients without diabetes, triangles test patients with it, and the red point is the patient.


Code for this plot (optional)
# every combination of glucose and BMI on a fine grid
grid <- expand_grid(glucose = seq(40, 200, by = 1),
                    mass = seq(18, 68, by = 0.5))

prob_map <- function(fit, title) {
  grid$prob <- predict(fit, new_data = grid, type = "prob")$.pred_pos
  ggplot(grid, aes(x = glucose, y = mass)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill = prob)) +
    geom_contour(aes(z = prob), breaks = 0.5, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_point(data = test, aes(shape = diabetes), size = 1.5) +
    annotate("point", x = 150, y = 30, colour = "red", size = 4) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "darkorange",
                         midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(neg = 1, pos = 17)) +
    labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "BMI (kg/m²)",
         fill = "Probability\nof diabetes", shape = "Test patients", title = title)
}

prob_map(log_fit_2, "Logistic regression: glucose and BMI")















ImportantThink about it




The line where the class changes is straight but tilted. What does the tilt tell you about BMI?
Adding BMI moved this patient from 0.547 to 0.490, and the class from pos to neg. Did BMI change much about this patient’s prediction?






Part 3 — The same steps, a decision tree
Only the specification changes. The training patients, the predictors and the fit() and predict() calls stay the same.

# 1. Specify: a classification tree, computed by rpart, kept small
tree_model <- decision_tree(tree_depth = 2, cost_complexity = 0) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# 2. Fit on the same training patients, with the same predictors
tree_fit <- tree_model |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass, data = train)

rpart.plot(tree_fit$fit, type = 3, extra = 106, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
           box.palette = "BuOr", roundint = FALSE)








tree_depth = 2 allows at most two questions in a row, and cost_complexity = 0 stops rpart from cutting the second question away.
Each box asks a yes/no question. Yes goes left, no goes right. Each leaf at the bottom shows three things: the predicted class, the probability of pos (the share of training patients in that leaf who have diabetes) and the percentage of all training patients who ended up there.

Task 3a — Follow the patient
Start at the top with the patient with a glucose of 150 and a BMI of 30. At each question, go left or right. Which leaf do you reach? What probability and what class does it give?
Check it with predict():

predict(tree_fit, new_data = patient, type = "prob")

#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   .pred_neg .pred_pos
#>       <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1     0.749     0.251

predict(tree_fit, new_data = patient)

#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   .pred_class
#>   <fct>      
#> 1 neg


The same map as for the logistic regression:


Code for this plot (optional)
prob_map(tree_fit, "Decision tree: glucose and BMI")









How often is each model right on the test patients?

data.frame(
  model = c("logistic, glucose", "logistic, glucose + BMI", "tree, glucose + BMI",
            "always says neg"),
  accuracy = c(mean(predict(log_fit,   new_data = test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes),
               mean(predict(log_fit_2, new_data = test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes),
               mean(predict(tree_fit,  new_data = test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes),
               mean(test$diabetes == "neg")))

#>                     model  accuracy
#> 1       logistic, glucose 0.7600000
#> 2 logistic, glucose + BMI 0.7600000
#> 3     tree, glucose + BMI 0.7333333
#> 4         always says neg 0.6466667








ImportantThink about it




The logistic regression gives every patient their own probability. How many different probabilities can the tree give, and why?
Compare the two maps. What shape is the region where each model says pos?
The three models gave the patient 0.55, 0.49 and 0.25. Their accuracies on the test patients are close. What does that tell you?









ImportantLearning points




The steps are the same as in Exercise 3.1: specify, fit on the training patients, predict for new ones. For a class instead of a number, only the mode in the specification changes.
predict() gives the class; predict(type = "prob") gives a probability for each class. The class is the probability cut at 0.5.
The probability carries more information than the class: near 0.5 a small change flips the class.
A logistic regression’s probability changes smoothly and its classes are split by a straight line; a tree gives one probability per leaf and splits the classes into rectangles.







Download this exercise as a Jupyter notebook (.ipynb): the text and every code cell of the Python version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in Jupyter or VS Code and run it a cell at a time.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree

data/diabetes_clean.csv holds 750 adults screened for type 2 diabetes: eight measurements from a single visit, and diabetes, which is pos or neg. It is ready to use. We keep glucose, BMI (the column mass) and the outcome. If you do not have it yet, download diabetes_clean.csv into your data folder.

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv")
diabetes = diabetes[["glucose", "mass", "diabetes"]]

diabetes.describe()

#>           glucose        mass
#> count  750.000000  750.000000
#> mean   125.496000   32.889467
#> std     31.405048    7.021630
#> min     57.000000   18.200000
#> 25%    101.000000   27.800000
#> 50%    119.000000   32.800000
#> 75%    145.000000   37.000000
#> max    196.000000   59.400000


We hold back every fifth person as the test set: 600 training patients and 150 test patients. Splitting by a fixed rule rather than at random gives both languages the same 150 people, so this tab prints the same numbers as the R tab. Every Day 4 exercise uses this split.

is_test = diabetes.index % 5 == 0               # every fifth person is held back
train = diabetes[~is_test]
test  = diabetes[is_test]

train["diabetes"].value_counts()

#> diabetes
#> neg    380
#> pos    220
#> Name: count, dtype: int64




Part 1 — Predict diabetes from glucose
The same three steps as in Exercise 3.1. The class name says that this model is for classification: LogisticRegression here, where Day 3 had LinearRegression.

# 1. Specify: logistic regression
log_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)

# 2. Fit on the training patients: predictors (a table) and outcome
log_model.fit(train[["glucose"]], train["diabetes"])

LogisticRegression(C=inf)In a Jupyter environment, please rerun this cell to show the HTML representation or trust the notebook. On GitHub, the HTML representation is unable to render, please try loading this page with nbviewer.org.LogisticRegression?Documentation for LogisticRegressioniFitted
        
            
                Parameters
                










C  C: float, default=1.0

Inverse of regularization strength; must be a positive float.
Like in support vector machines, smaller values specify stronger
regularization. `C=np.inf` results in unpenalized logistic regression.
For a visual example on the effect of tuning the `C` parameter
with an L1 penalty, see:
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_logistic_path.py`.
inf




penalty  penalty: {'l1', 'l2', 'elasticnet', None}, default='l2'

Specify the norm of the penalty:

- `None`: no penalty is added;
- `'l2'`: add an L2 penalty term and it is the default choice;
- `'l1'`: add an L1 penalty term;
- `'elasticnet'`: both L1 and L2 penalty terms are added.

.. warning::
Some penalties may not work with some solvers. See the parameter
`solver` below, to know the compatibility between the penalty and
solver.

.. versionadded:: 0.19
l1 penalty with SAGA solver (allowing 'multinomial' + L1)

.. deprecated:: 1.8
`penalty` was deprecated in version 1.8 and will be removed in 1.10.
Use `l1_ratio` and `C` instead. `l1_ratio=0` for `penalty='l2'`,
`l1_ratio=1` for `penalty='l1'`, `l1_ratio` set to any float between 0 and 1
for `penalty='elasticnet'`, and `C=np.inf` for `penalty=None`.
'deprecated'




l1_ratio  l1_ratio: float, default=0.0

The Elastic-Net mixing parameter, with `0 <= l1_ratio <= 1`. Setting
`l1_ratio=1` gives a pure L1-penalty, setting `l1_ratio=0` a pure L2-penalty.
Any value between 0 and 1 gives an Elastic-Net penalty of the form
`l1_ratio * L1 + (1 - l1_ratio) * L2`.

.. warning::
Certain values of `l1_ratio`, i.e. some penalties, may not work with some
solvers. See the parameter `solver` below, to know the compatibility between
the penalty and solver.

.. versionchanged:: 1.8
Default value changed from None to 0.0.

.. deprecated:: 1.8
`None` is deprecated and will be removed in version 1.10. Always use
`l1_ratio` to specify the penalty type.
0.0




dual  dual: bool, default=False

Dual (constrained) or primal (regularized, see also
:ref:`this equation <regularized-logistic-loss>`) formulation. Dual formulation
is only implemented for l2 penalty with liblinear solver. Prefer `dual=False`
when n_samples > n_features.
False




tol  tol: float, default=1e-4

Tolerance for stopping criteria.
0.0001




fit_intercept  fit_intercept: bool, default=True

Specifies if a constant (a.k.a. bias or intercept) should be
added to the decision function.
True




intercept_scaling  intercept_scaling: float, default=1

Useful only when the solver `liblinear` is used
and `self.fit_intercept` is set to `True`. In this case, `x` becomes
`[x, self.intercept_scaling]`,
i.e. a "synthetic" feature with constant value equal to
`intercept_scaling` is appended to the instance vector.
The intercept becomes
``intercept_scaling * synthetic_feature_weight``.

.. note::
The synthetic feature weight is subject to L1 or L2
regularization as all other features.
To lessen the effect of regularization on synthetic feature weight
(and therefore on the intercept) `intercept_scaling` has to be increased.
1




class_weight  class_weight: dict or 'balanced', default=None

Weights associated with classes in the form ``{class_label: weight}``.
If not given, all classes are supposed to have weight one.

The "balanced" mode uses the values of y to automatically adjust
weights inversely proportional to class frequencies in the input data
as ``n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))``.

Note that these weights will be multiplied with sample_weight (passed
through the fit method) if sample_weight is specified.

.. versionadded:: 0.17
*class_weight='balanced'*
None




random_state  random_state: int, RandomState instance, default=None

Only used for `solver` == 'sag', 'saga' or 'liblinear' to shuffle the
data. It has no effect on the other solvers.
See :term:`Glossary <random_state>` for details.
None




solver  solver: {'lbfgs', 'liblinear', 'newton-cg', 'newton-cholesky', 'sag', 'saga'}, default='lbfgs'

Algorithm to use in the optimization problem. Default is 'lbfgs'.
To choose a solver, you might want to consider the following aspects:

- 'lbfgs' is a good default solver because it works reasonably well for a wide
class of problems.
- For :term:`multiclass` problems (`n_classes >= 3`), all solvers except
'liblinear' minimize the full multinomial loss, 'liblinear' will raise an
error.
- 'newton-cholesky' is a good choice for
`n_samples` >> `n_features * n_classes`, especially with one-hot encoded
categorical features with rare categories. Be aware that the memory usage
of this solver has a quadratic dependency on `n_features * n_classes`
because it explicitly computes the full Hessian matrix.
- For small datasets, 'liblinear' is a good choice, whereas 'sag'
and 'saga' are faster for large ones;
- 'liblinear' can only handle binary classification by default. To apply a
one-versus-rest scheme for the multiclass setting one can wrap it with the
:class:`~sklearn.multiclass.OneVsRestClassifier`.

.. warning::
The choice of the algorithm depends on the penalty chosen (`l1_ratio=0`
for L2-penalty, `l1_ratio=1` for L1-penalty and `0 < l1_ratio < 1` for
Elastic-Net) and on (multinomial) multiclass support:

================= ======================== ======================
solver l1_ratio multinomial multiclass
================= ======================== ======================
'lbfgs' l1_ratio=0 yes
'liblinear' l1_ratio=1 or l1_ratio=0 no
'newton-cg' l1_ratio=0 yes
'newton-cholesky' l1_ratio=0 yes
'sag' l1_ratio=0 yes
'saga' 0<=l1_ratio<=1 yes
================= ======================== ======================

.. note::
'sag' and 'saga' fast convergence is only guaranteed on features
with approximately the same scale. You can preprocess the data with
a scaler from :mod:`sklearn.preprocessing`.

.. seealso::
Refer to the :ref:`User Guide <Logistic_regression>` for more
information regarding :class:`LogisticRegression` and more specifically the
:ref:`Table <logistic_regression_solvers>`
summarizing solver/penalty supports.

.. versionadded:: 0.17
Stochastic Average Gradient (SAG) descent solver. Multinomial support in
version 0.18.
.. versionadded:: 0.19
SAGA solver.
.. versionchanged:: 0.22
The default solver changed from 'liblinear' to 'lbfgs' in 0.22.
.. versionadded:: 1.2
newton-cholesky solver. Multinomial support in version 1.6.
'lbfgs'




max_iter  max_iter: int, default=100

Maximum number of iterations taken for the solvers to converge.
100




verbose  verbose: int, default=0

For the liblinear and lbfgs solvers set verbose to any positive
number for verbosity.
0




warm_start  warm_start: bool, default=False

When set to True, reuse the solution of the previous call to fit as
initialization, otherwise, just erase the previous solution.
Useless for liblinear solver. See :term:`the Glossary <warm_start>`.

.. versionadded:: 0.17
*warm_start* to support *lbfgs*, *newton-cg*, *sag*, *saga* solvers.
False




n_jobs  n_jobs: int, default=None

Does not have any effect.

.. deprecated:: 1.8
`n_jobs` is deprecated in version 1.8 and will be removed in 1.10.
None




            
        
    
        
            
                Fitted attributes
                








Name
Type
Value


classes_  classes_: ndarray of shape (n_classes, )

A list of class labels known to the classifier.
ndarray[object](2,)
['neg','pos']


coef_  coef_: ndarray or CSR matrix of shape (1, n_features) or (n_classes, n_features)

Coefficients of the features in the decision function.

`coef_` is of shape (1, n_features) when the given problem is binary.

By default, it will be created as a dense array, but can be turned to
sparse (CSR format) through :meth:`sparsify` (which can be beneficial
under L1 regularization when many coefficients are zero), and back to
dense through :meth:`densify`.
ndarray[float64](1, 1)
[[0.04]]


feature_names_in_  feature_names_in_: ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)

Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
has feature names that are all strings.

.. versionadded:: 1.0
ndarray[object](1,)
['glucose']


intercept_  intercept_: ndarray of shape (1,) or (n_classes,)

Intercept (a.k.a. bias) added to the decision function.

If `fit_intercept` is set to False, the intercept is set to zero.
`intercept_` is of shape (1,) when the given problem is binary.
ndarray[float64](1,)
[-5.06]


n_features_in_  n_features_in_: int

Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.

.. versionadded:: 0.24
int
1


n_iter_  n_iter_: ndarray of shape (1, )

Actual number of iterations for all classes.

.. versionchanged:: 0.20

In SciPy <= 1.0.0 the number of lbfgs iterations may exceed
``max_iter``. ``n_iter_`` will now report at most ``max_iter``.
ndarray[int32](1,)
[21]




            
        
    

# the classes, and the learned parameters
print("classes:", log_model.classes_)

#> classes: ['neg' 'pos']

print("intercept:", log_model.intercept_)

#> intercept: [-5.0639797]

print("weight for glucose:", log_model.coef_)

#> weight for glucose: [[0.03502648]]


C=np.inf switches off a penalty that scikit-learn adds to logistic regression by default; without it the parameters would not match the ones in the R tab.
The two parameters are not on the glucose scale but on the log-odds scale. Exercise 4.2 shows how they turn into a probability. Here we let scikit-learn do it.

Task 1a — A patient with a glucose of 150

The probabilities change; the classes do not.

Code for this plot (optional)
prob_map(tree_model, "Decision tree: glucose and BMI")









How often is each model right on the test patients?

pd.DataFrame({
    "model": ["logistic, glucose", "logistic, glucose + BMI", "tree, glucose + BMI",
              "always says neg"],
    "accuracy": [log_model.score(test[["glucose"]], test["diabetes"]),
                 log_model_2.score(test[["glucose", "mass"]], test["diabetes"]),
                 tree_model.score(test[["glucose", "mass"]], test["diabetes"]),
                 (test["diabetes"] == "neg").mean()]})

#>                      model  accuracy
#> 0        logistic, glucose  0.760000
#> 1  logistic, glucose + BMI  0.760000
#> 2      tree, glucose + BMI  0.733333
#> 3          always says neg  0.646667


.score() is the accuracy: the share of patients whose predicted class is right.






ImportantThink about it




The logistic regression gives every patient their own probability. How many different probabilities can the tree give, and why?
Compare the two maps. What shape is the region where each model says pos?
The three models gave the patient 0.55, 0.49 and 0.31. Their accuracies on the test patients are close. What does that tell you?









ImportantLearning points




The steps are the same as in Exercise 3.1: specify, fit on the training patients, predict for new ones. For a class instead of a number, only the estimator changes: LogisticRegression and DecisionTreeClassifier.
.predict() gives the class; .predict_proba() gives a probability for each class. The class is the probability cut at 0.5.
The probability carries more information than the class: near 0.5 a small change flips the class.
A logistic regression’s probability changes smoothly and its classes are split by a straight line; a tree gives one probability per leaf and splits the classes into rectangles.

title: Exercise 4.2 — Fitting a logistic regression model
text:
Stretch
Linear regression on Day 3 predicted a number, glucose. Logistic regression predicts a probability: the chance that a person has diabetes, given their glucose. A probability must stay between 0 and 1, and a straight line does not. The trick is to fit the straight line on a different scale, the log-odds, and convert back.
Theory: probability, odds and log-odds; the logistic (sigmoid) function; reading a logistic regression coefficient; from a fitted model to a probability.

title: Exercise 4.3 — The decision threshold
text:
Stretch
A logistic regression outputs a probability,
\[\hat{p}(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid x),\]
but a clinic needs a decision: test this person for diabetes, or not. To turn the probability into a predicted class we choose a decision threshold. Usually:
But 0.5 is arbitrary. Changing the threshold changes how many true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives the model makes, and so which mistakes it makes.
Theory: decision threshold; confusion table; true and false positives and negatives; sensitivity and specificity; the cost of each kind of mistake.

title: Exercise 4.3 — The decision threshold
text:
NoteStretch — choose the threshold honestly



The cheapest threshold above was chosen by looking at the test patients, and then judged on the same test patients. Choose it on the training rows instead, then apply it once to the test patients. Is the cost still 71? Why is this the honest way round?

title: Exercise 4.4 — Is a predicted 0.7 worth 0.7?
text:
Stretch
Exercise 4.3 chose a threshold of 0.2 because of what each mistake costs. That choice assumed something it never checked: that among the people the model gives a probability of about 0.2, about 20% really do have diabetes. A model whose probabilities match what happens in this way is calibrated.
Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity cannot tell you whether a model is calibrated, because they throw the probability away at the threshold and only look at the predicted classes.
Theory: calibration in the large; the calibration table and curve; why small groups give noisy rates; the Brier score; a model that ranks people well can still give the wrong probabilities.
